analysis.one_liner: Requires chemical hazard information sheets be written in both English and Spanish.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with 3 cosponsors in July 2024, it was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee and died there when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the Occupational Safety and Health Act to require that safety data sheets — the documents that explain what chemicals workers are exposed to and how to handle them safely — be written in both English and Spanish. Chemical manufacturers and importers would have to produce the bilingual sheets and give them to employers, who would have to make them accessible to exposed workers. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers exposed to hazardous chemicals who read Spanish — a large share of the workforce in agriculture, construction, cleaning, and food processing — would get the hazard information they need in a language they can read, which should mean fewer poisonings, burns, and long-term illnesses. Employers would also benefit from a safer, better-informed workforce and potentially fewer injury claims.

how_it_helps.text: Safety data sheets — the required write-ups of what a chemical is, how it can hurt you, and what to do about it — would have to be produced in both English and Spanish by the manufacturer or importer, so Spanish-speaking workers could actually read the warnings.

Employers would receive the bilingual sheets and would be required to make them accessible to employees exposed to the hazard, closing the gap between a warning existing somewhere in a file and a worker being able to read it.

The requirement would apply to any OSHA chemical-safety standard issued or changed before or after enactment, taking effect 60 days after the bill became law — so it would reach existing standards, not just future ones.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and importers would bear the cost of producing safety data sheets in two languages and supplying them to employers, and employers of chemically exposed workers would bear a modest cost of storing and making those sheets accessible. The costs are small relative to a document-production process most companies already run.

drawbacks.text: Chemical manufacturers and importers would take on the cost of producing and distributing every safety data sheet in two languages and getting them to employers.

The bill only requires English and Spanish. Workers who read neither — for example speakers of other languages common in some industries — would remain dependent on translated versions no one is required to provide.
The requirement reaches standards issued before enactment and kicks in 60 days after the bill became law, so manufacturers would face a fast turnaround to retrofit existing documents.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — workers being able to read instructions for handling chemicals that can burn, poison, or sicken them — is real and falls on people with little power in the workplace; the cost, double-language document production, is modest and routine for companies already required to author these sheets. The honest caveat is scope: a fixed English-Spanish requirement helps a large group but not all workers who struggle with English-only sheets.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Cuellar introduced the bill on July 11, 2024, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
Three Democratic colleagues signed on as cosponsors, but no further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, the bill died, as any bill that has not passed both chambers does.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers and importers avoid a bilingual-sheet requirement, and employers avoid a small compliance burden. Spanish-speaking workers exposed to hazardous chemicals remain without a federal guarantee that the safety information about those chemicals is written in a language they read.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical makers; exposed Spanish-speaking workers unchanged

for.name: Rep. Henry Cuellar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

for.name: 3 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill stayed in committee until it died.

sides.party_line_note: It never reached a vote, so no one had to take a public position; all four members attached to the bill (the sponsor and 3 cosponsors) were Democrats.

industries.note: They would have to produce safety data sheets in English and Spanish and supply them to employers. The cost is modest — it is a second-language version of a document they already must write — but the industry's interest in avoiding it runs against workers being able to read hazard warnings.

industries.industry: Employers of chemically exposed workforces (agriculture, construction, cleaning, food processing)
industries.note: They would bear a small cost receiving and making bilingual sheets accessible, but a workforce that can read the warnings means fewer injuries and less downtime, which serves employers too.
